psalms/1.sum: Two ways, side by side: the righteous (A), the wicked (B), then one verse that holds both.

parts.t: The righteous: a tree planted by water
The wicked: chaff the wind blows away
The LORD guards the path of the righteous
The way of the wicked will perish

notes: Verse 1 builds: walk, then stand ("set foot"), then sit. Each step settles in deeper.
In Hebrew the first word begins with aleph and the last word begins with taw, the first and last letters of the alphabet: the whole life, A to Z.
The word "way" (derek) appears only in the first and last verses, framing the psalm.

psalms/8.sum: The same line opens and closes the psalm (A ... A'), like bookends around the middle.

parts.t: Bookend: how majestic is Your name
God's glory, the heavens, and what is man?
Man crowned and given rule over creation

ref: how majestic is Your name in all the earth
notes: A repeated opening and closing is called an inclusio. It tells you what the whole poem is about: the greatness of God's name, not of man.
The question in verse 4 ("what is man?") is the turning point. Hebrews 2:6-9 reads verses 4-6 as fulfilled in Jesus.

psalms/23.sum: God goes before (A), beside (B) and behind (C) the psalmist. "For You are with me" sits at the exact middle.

parts.t: Beside me: in the dark valley (You)
The host: a table, oil and a full cup (You)
Behind me: goodness and mercy follow

notes: Count the Hebrew words: 26 come before "for You are with me" and 26 come after it. The poem puts God's presence at its center.
Listen for the switch: verses 1-3 talk about God ("He"); from verse 4 the psalmist talks to God ("You"). The danger is where the prayer becomes personal.
"Follow" in verse 6 is the Hebrew radaph, usually "pursue" or "chase". Goodness and mercy hunt him down.

psalms/34.sum: Each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, aleph to taw, with one twist at the end.
notes: There is no line for waw, the sixth letter, and an extra pe line closes the psalm. Psalm 25 has the same two quirks, so it looks deliberate.
With the extra pe, lamedh ("Come, children, listen to me", verse 11) lands in the middle, and the first, middle and last letters spell aleph, the name of the first letter.
English verse numbers are one lower than the Hebrew, which counts the title as verse 1.

psalms/42.sum: A refrain closes each stanza. The same refrain ends Psalm 43, which completes this poem.

parts.t: Stanza 1: thirst for God, memories of the festival

ref: Why are you downcast, O my soul
notes: Psalm 43 has no title of its own and ends with the same refrain (43:5). Some Hebrew manuscripts copy 42 and 43 as one psalm.
The refrain is the psalmist talking to himself: he answers his feelings with hope instead of letting them talk to him.

psalms/43.sum: The third stanza of the poem that starts in Psalm 42, closing with the same refrain.

parts.t: Stanza 3: send out Your light and truth

ref: Why are you downcast, O my soul
notes: Read 42:1 to 43:5 straight through: three stanzas, three refrains, moving from longing to asking to going up to God's altar.

psalms/46.sum: Three stanzas, each ending in "Selah". The second and third close with the same refrain.

parts.t: Stanza 1: the earth shakes, we will not fear
Stanza 2: the river and the city of God
Stanza 3: come and see; be still

ref: The LORD of Hosts is with us
the God of Jacob is our fortress
notes: The poem moves from chaos (roaring waters) to a calm river (verse 4) to God speaking (verse 10).
"Selah" marks a pause or musical break. No one knows its exact meaning, but here it marks the end of each stanza.

psalms/67.sum: A mirror pattern, A B C B' A'. The outer lines match, the refrain repeats, and the middle line is the point.

parts.t: Bless us, so Your way is known on earth
Refrain: let the peoples praise You
Center: You judge the peoples justly
The earth has yielded; God blesses us

ref: Let the peoples praise You, O God
let all the peoples praise You
notes: Verse 1 borrows the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26 ("make His face shine upon us"), then turns it outward to the nations.
In a chiasm the center usually carries the main idea. Here it is God ruling every nation fairly.

psalms/119.sum: 22 stanzas, one for each Hebrew letter. All 8 lines of a stanza begin with that stanza's letter.
notes: 176 verses: 22 letters times 8. It is the longest chapter in the Bible.
Nearly every verse names God's word with one of about eight terms: law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, judgments, word, promise.
Older English Bibles print the letter names (ALEPH, BETH ...) as headings over each stanza.

psalms/136.sum: Every verse ends with the same response. A leader likely sang the first half and the people answered.

parts.t: God who brought Israel out of Egypt
Through the wilderness and into the land

notes: 26 times in 26 verses. "Loving devotion" is the Hebrew hesed: loyal, covenant love that does not quit.
Jewish tradition calls this psalm the Great Hallel and sings it at Passover.

psalms/145.sum: Each verse starts with the next Hebrew letter. The nun line is missing from the standard Hebrew text.
notes: The traditional Hebrew text skips nun. A Dead Sea Scroll (11QPs-a) and the Greek translation have a nun line, and the BSB includes it as the second half of verse 13.
Jewish prayer calls this psalm Ashrei and prays it three times a day.

psalms/150.sum: "Hallelujah" bookends the psalm. In between: where to praise, why, with what, and who.

parts.t: Where: His sanctuary and the heavens
Why: His mighty acts and greatness

notes: Each of the five books of Psalms ends with a doxology. Psalm 150 is the doxology for the whole book.
"Hallelujah" means "Praise Yah", a short form of the LORD's name.

proverbs/31.sum: The poem of the noble wife runs aleph to taw: 22 verses, one per Hebrew letter.

parts.t: King Lemuel's mother: advice to a king

notes: The alphabet shape says "this is the complete picture": wisdom lived out from A to Z.

"Noble character" (hayil) is the word used for strength and valor in battle. Ruth is the only woman the Bible names as a woman of hayil (Ruth 3:11), and in the Hebrew order Ruth comes right after Proverbs.

ecclesiastes/3.sum: One thesis line, then 14 pairs of opposites: 28 "times" in all.

parts.t: The thesis: a season for everything
The Teacher reflects on the poem

notes: The list opens with birth and death, the widest pair of all, and closes with war and peace.
Many readers see 14 (two times seven) as a sign of completeness: every season of life is covered, and none of it is outside God's timing (verse 11).
